newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Eastbrokers says Hungary gas shares are good buy.
newsitem.headline: Eastbrokers says Hungary gas shares are good buy.

text.p: Hungarian gas utility shares are likely to offer attractive buying opportunities to portfolio investors in the first half of 1997, Hungarian brokerage Eastbrokers said in a recent research study.

"Portfolio investors should be able to purchase these gas utility shares at highly attractive prices in the coming months," the study said, adding that the price of the shares was likely to be at or below the net asset value (NAV).
"According to our projections, if shares trade at NAV, earnings per share should run 10 to 13 percent of the dollar purchase price by 1998 for all the companies," it said.
Hungary's regional gas distribution companies were partly sold to western investors in 1995 and 1996.
Cash-strapped local municipalities will receive 40 percent of each of five gas utilities in the next few months, while the capital Budapest holds the majority of the city's gas distributor, Fogaz.
Eastbrokers said some municipalities had already used their shares as collateral for loans needed to fund local projects, while other stocks were likely to be dumped on the market.

The brokerage said that in contrast to those in other emerging markets, Hungarian companies did not need to invest heavily in hooking up new households to the network, making cash flows from these companies attractive, as over 70 percent of households had already access to piped gas.

The research recommended investors to buy the shares of the larger gas utilities, Fogaz, Degaz and Tigaz. These firms would be the lowest cost distributors as they were able to spread overheads over a larger client base.
Eastbrokers said the most attractive of the stocks was Fogaz as it had a very compact distribution network, making developments cheap, and it also had a large share of industrial sales.

The brokerage forecast industrial gas sales to rise by almost 50 percent to 5.1 billion cubic meters between 1994 and 2000, while household demand was projected to increase by 8.8 percent to 3.3 billion cubic meters between 1995 and 2000.
